name: Thymic epithelial cell
summary: The framework cell of the thymus. Epithelial cells form a mesh that developing T cells move through. In the cortex they keep T cells whose receptors can recognise the body's own MHC molecules. In the medulla they display proteins made all over the body, so strongly self-reactive T cells are removed or become regulatory T cells.
functions: Forms the framework of the thymus: a three-dimensional mesh of cortical and medullary epithelial cells that developing T cells (thymocytes) crawl through. All depend on the transcription factor FOXN1; mice and people without a working copy lack a functional thymus and have almost no T cells.

Supports the first steps of T-cell development in the cortex: cortical epithelial cells carry the Notch ligand DLL4, which pushes arriving progenitors to become T cells, and make growth signals such as IL-7. Chemokines such as CCL25 help draw progenitors in. Shown mainly in mice.

Runs positive selection in the cortex: cortical epithelial cells show self-peptides on MHC class I and class II. A thymocyte whose receptor binds them with the right, fairly weak strength gets a survival signal and commits to the CD4 or CD8 line, according to which MHC it bound; most thymocytes bind nothing and die. Cortical cells make their peptides with thymus-specific enzymes (the thymoproteasome subunit β5t for MHC class I; cathepsin L and thymus-specific serine protease for MHC class II), shown mainly in mice.

Teaches the body's own proteins in the medulla: medullary epithelial cells switch on thousands of genes normally active only in other organs, many of them controlled by AIRE (and in mice also FEZF2), and show the peptides on MHC. T cells that react strongly are deleted (negative selection) or diverted to become regulatory T cells. They also hand proteins on to dendritic cells, which then present them too, widening the range of self-antigens each T cell is checked against. People with AIRE mutations develop autoimmunity in several organs (the syndrome APECED).

Helps make regulatory T cells: CD4 thymocytes that bind self-peptide on medullary epithelial cells fairly strongly can switch on FOXP3 instead of dying. In mice a missing or disorganised medulla gives fewer regulatory T cells.
Guides thymocytes from cortex to medulla: positively selected thymocytes switch on the chemokine receptor CCR7 and follow CCL19 and CCL21 made by the medullary epithelium (shown in mice).

Debated: how many kinds of thymic epithelial cell there are. The textbook picture has two, cortical and medullary, but single-cell studies of mouse and human thymus describe further subsets (for example tuft-like and muscle-like medullary cells) and it is not settled which are fixed types and which are stages.

Debated: where the lines fall between survival, death and regulatory T-cell fate. The textbook model (weak signal, survive; strong signal, die or become regulatory T cell) is widely accepted, but how thymocytes read the signal, and how much cortical and medullary cells differ in what they offer, is still argued. Most evidence is from mice.

Debated: what Hassall's corpuscles, whorls of medullary epithelial cells first described in human thymus and different in other species, actually do. Work on human thymus tissue found they make TSLP, which conditions dendritic cells to induce regulatory T cells in culture; whether they do this in the living thymus is unconfirmed.
abundance: A small minority of the cells in the thymus: developing T cells far outnumber them, yet the epithelial mesh does most of the selecting. The thymus is largest in childhood; from puberty its epithelial space shrinks and is replaced by fat (involution) and output of new T cells falls, though it does not stop. Most detailed counts and subset studies come from mice.
